module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Fibonacci Primes

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_prime)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace FibonacciPrimes

/--
There are infinitely many Fibonacci primes, i.e., Fibonacci numbers that are prime
It is also a barrier to defining a benchmark from this paper:
https://arxiv.org/html/2505.13938v1 (see Figure 8).

-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem fib_primes_infinite : {n : ℕ | (∃ m : ℕ, m.fib = n) ∧ n.Prime}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
There are infinitely many indices $i$, such that the $i$-th Fibonacci is prime.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem fib_primes_infinite.variant : {n : ℕ | n.fib.Prime}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
The two ways of phrasing the conjecture are equivalent.
-/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem indices_infinite_iff_fib_primes_infinite : type_of% fib_primes_infinite.variant ↔
    type_of% fib_primes_infinite := by
  simp only [Set.infinite_iff_exists_gt]
  constructor
  · intros h a
    rcases h (a + 1) with ⟨b', ⟨hb₁, hb₂⟩⟩
    use Nat.fib b'
    exact ⟨⟨exists_apply_eq_apply Nat.fib b', hb₁⟩,
      by linear_combination b'.le_fib_add_one + hb₂⟩
  · intro h a
    rcases h (Nat.fib a) with ⟨b', ⟨⟨m, hm⟩, hb₁⟩, hb₂⟩
    use m
    constructor
    · simp_all
    · have := @m.fib_mono a
      omega

end FibonacciPrimes

reformulations.difference: The source asks whether there are infinitely many Fibonacci primes, i.e. prime values of the Fibonacci sequence. The variant instead says that the set of indices n with `Nat.fib n` prime is infinite.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: `Nat.fib` is strictly increasing on n ≥ 2, and F_0 = 0, F_1 = F_2 = 1 are not prime. So n ↦ F_n is a bijection from the prime-index set onto the set of Fibonacci primes, and one set is infinite iff the other is. The file's own test theorem `indices_infinite_iff_fib_primes_infinite` proves exactly `{n | (Nat.fib n).Prime}.Infinite ↔ {n | (∃ m, Nat.fib m = n) ∧ n.Prime}.Infinite`. I checked with `#print axioms` that it uses only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, with no sorryAx.

sources_consulted: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics (raw wikitext; entry 'Are there infinitely many Fibonacci primes?')
https://arxiv.org/html/2505.13938v1 (Figure 8 caption and listings: '(b) Prime Fibonacci finder: problem complexity rooted in the lack of a known proof of infinitude')
Mathlib source: .lake/packages/mathlib/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Fib/Basic.lean (definition of Nat.fib, fib_zero/one/two, fib_strictMonoOn)
review.notes:
No defects found. Checks I made:
(1) `#check`/`#print` confirm `fib_primes_infinite : {n | (∃ m, Nat.fib m = n) ∧ Nat.Prime n}.Infinite` and `fib_primes_infinite.variant : {n | Nat.Prime (Nat.fib n)}.Infinite`.
(2) Boundary cases, verified in Lean: 0 and 1 are Fibonacci numbers but are excluded because they are not prime; 2 and 89 are in the value set; 4 is in the index set and 19 is not (F_19 = 4181 = 37·113).
(3) `#eval` gives prime indices below 60 as [3, 4, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 23, 29, 43, 47], the same as Wikipedia's A001605 list. Mathlib's F_1 = F_2 = 1 indexing matches Wikipedia's.
(4) The test theorem proving the two forms equivalent is sorry-free.
(5) Status: Wikipedia and MathWorld both still say it is unknown whether there are infinitely many Fibonacci primes, so `research open` is correct.
(6) The docstring's pointer to Figure 8 of arXiv 2505.13938v1 is accurate.

Style only, not a defect: Wikipedia poses this as a question. The file asserts the conjectured positive answer directly (Wikipedia's infobox gives the conjectured number of terms as 'Infinite') rather than using `answer(sorry) ↔ P`. The repository uses both styles for similar problems: plain `P` in Pell.lean, WoodalPrimes.lean and WieferichPrime.lean, and `answer(sorry) ↔` in TwinPrimes.lean, Mersenne.lean and Fermat.lean. The mathematical content is the same either way.

OEIS pages A005478/A001605 were behind a Cloudflare challenge, so I could not read them directly. I used Wikipedia's copy of the A001605 terms instead.
